Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Speko
Speko MCP is the authenticated operational interface for Speko voice-AI accounts.

Use these tools to inspect organization state, manage agents, deploy versions, create sessions and phone calls, retrieve transcripts and recordings, manage phone numbers and knowledge bases, run evals, and build or migrate SessionConfig drafts.

Docs are available in-band: call docs.search(query) to find SDK usage, API body shapes, and migration steps across the bundled Speko docs, then read the matching spekoai://docs/{slug} resource. spekoai://docs/index lists every bundled doc. If a write tool rejects a body, search the failing field name before retrying.

All tools require the hosted MCP endpoint at /mcp. Interactive clients may use OAuth; automation may supply a Speko API key as Authorization: Bearer sk_*. Tool names use domain.action dot notation, for example agents.list, sessions.create, docs.search, and knowledge_bases.documents.create.

When the user is blocked by something only the Speko team can fix (an error says to contact support, a feature is not enabled for the workspace, a billing problem, or a platform bug), offer to open a ticket with support.ticket.create instead of sending them to email. Put the trace_id and any agent, session or call ids in the ticket, and give the user the ticketUrl it returns. The team replies on the ticket: a result warning SUPPORT_REPLY_UNREAD means a reply is waiting, read it with support.ticket.get and answer with support.ticket.reply. Tickets are only for problems with Speko itself, never for the assistant or another product. Show the user the exact summary and details and get their yes before calling support.ticket.create, and leave out personal details the Speko problem does not need.

Using a carrier or VoIP number the user already has (Twilio, Telnyx, Vonage) needs no ticket and no SIP gateway: connect it with phone_numbers.sip_connections.create then phone_numbers.import, or the dashboard's Import number > Add carrier connection. The SIP gateway is only for a PBX.

# Project rules for Claude Code

This repo is graded on two things: the dApp, and how well we audit the code AI tools wrote for it. The process below exists so every claim in our AI Audit Report has evidence behind it. Follow it even when it feels slower.

## Before writing any code

- Read `docs/spec/spec-v1.md` first.
- If it still contains `TODO(decision)` markers, the spec is not frozen. Do not write contract code. Say which decisions are still open and stop.
- Every function you write must trace to a section of the spec. If the spec is silent or ambiguous on something you need, stop and ask. Do not invent requirements.

## Branches and tags

- Never commit to, rebase, or rewrite the `ai-baseline` branch, or move the `spec-v0` or `ai-baseline` tags.
- Never amend published commits or force-push.

## When a bug, vulnerability or spec gap is found

1. Run `scripts/new-issue.sh "<short title>"`. This creates `docs/issues/AUD-NNN-*.md`.
2. Write a regression test that FAILS on the current code. Commit it alone as `test(AUD-NNN): ...`.
3. Run `scripts/evidence.sh AUD-NNN-before`.
4. Fix the code. Commit as `fix(AUD-NNN): ...`.
5. Run `scripts/evidence.sh AUD-NNN-after`.
6. Fill in all four sections of the issue file. Do not set Status to fixed without both evidence runs.

In "Why the AI made the mistake", only state what the transcript or code shows. If you are guessing, start the line with `Hypothesis:`.

## Secrets

- Never read `.env` or print private keys, RPC keys or API keys. AI transcripts in this repo are committed to git.
- Only testnet burner wallets are used in this project.

## Commit message prefixes

| Prefix | Use for |
|---|---|
| `ai:` | Code generated by an AI tool and committed with little or no human change |
| `human:` | Code written or substantially rewritten by a person |
| `test(AUD-NNN):` | Regression test for an issue |
| `fix(AUD-NNN):` | Fix for an issue |
| `docs:` | Spec, report, issue files |
| `evidence:` | Evidence runs, testnet logs |
| `chore:` | Tooling and config |

## Rules learned from audit findings

Append a rule here each time an audit finding shows the AI making a mistake it could repeat. Every rule must cite the issue it came from. This section is part of our specification engineering evidence, so never delete old rules; mark them superseded instead.

- (none yet)

1	# Setting up the evidence pipeline
2	
3	Do the steps in order. Step 2 has to happen before any AI tool touches the repo.
4	
5	## 0. Installs (each teammate, once)
6	
7	- Git and Python 3.8 or newer
8	- Foundry: `curl -L https://foundry.paradigm.xyz | bash`, then `foundryup`
9	- Slither: `python3 -m pip install slither-analyzer`
10	- Your git name, which is recorded on every evidence run and AI session: `git config --global user.name "Your Name"`
11	
12	If `python3` is not the command for Python on your machine, change the two `"python3"` entries in `.claude/settings.json`.
13	
14	## 1. Create the repo
15	
16	Make it a **private** GitHub repo. AI transcripts are committed, and they can contain anything that was typed into a session. Clone it.
17	
18	## 2. Commit spec v0 first, on its own
19	
20	Unzip this kit into the repo root. Fill in "Date written" and "Written by" in `docs/spec/spec-v0.md`. Then:
21	
22	```bash
23	git add docs/spec/spec-v0.md
24	git commit -m "docs: spec v0 (pre-AI proposal)"
25	git tag spec-v0
26	git add -A
27	git commit -m "chore: evidence pipeline"
28	git push --follow-tags
29	```
30	
31	Be honest about what this proves. Git commit dates can be set to anything, so the tag alone is weak evidence. The strong evidence is the date you submitted the BYOP proposal to the coordinator, so put that date in the file.
32	
33	## 3. Log today's research chat
34	
35	Copy the claude.ai conversation from 23 Oct 2026 into `docs/ai-logs/exports/2026-10-23-claude-ai-research.md`. Its row in `docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md` is already filled in.
36	
37	## 4. Start Claude Code and check the hook
38	
39	From the repo root run `claude -n toolchain-setup`. Accept the trust prompt for the folder if one appears. Run `/hooks`: it should list a `Stop` hook and a `SessionEnd` hook from project settings. After Claude's first reply, `docs/ai-logs/raw/` should contain a `.jsonl` file. If it doesn't, stop and fix that first, because every session before the fix is lost evidence.
40	
41	## 5. Paste this prompt into Claude Code
42	
43	```text
44	Read CLAUDE.md first. Set up the Foundry toolchain for this repo. Do not write any contract code: spec-v1 is not frozen.
45	
46	1. Check that forge and slither are installed (forge --version, slither --version). If either is missing, stop and tell me. Don't install them yourself.
47	2. Run `forge init --force` in the repo root. Then run `git status` and make sure it did not change .gitignore, CLAUDE.md, SETUP.md, slither.config.json, or anything under docs/, scripts/ or .claude/. Restore anything it changed.
48	3. Install OpenZeppelin Contracts pinned to the latest v5.x release tag. Find the tag with `git ls-remote --tags https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts`, then `forge install OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts@<tag>`. Write remappings with `forge remappings > remappings.txt`.
49	4. Make the scripts executable: chmod +x scripts/*.sh .claude/hooks/archive_transcript.py
50	5. Run `scripts/evidence.sh pipeline-check` and show me summary.txt. build, test, gas and coverage should exit 0. Slither exits non-zero only if it reports findings.
51	6. Delete src/Counter.sol, test/Counter.t.sol and script/Counter.s.sol so the AI baseline starts from an empty src/.
52	7. Commit everything as "chore: foundry toolchain and OpenZeppelin <tag>". Do not push.
53	
54	Then tell me what you did and anything that did not go as described.
55	```
56	
57	## 6. After the session
58	
59	Run `/export docs/ai-logs/exports/<date>-toolchain-setup.txt` before you quit. Add a row to `docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md`. Commit and push.
60	
61	## Later: creating the AI baseline
62	
63	Once `spec-v1.md` has no `TODO(decision)` left, generate the first full version of the contracts on its own branch and freeze it:
64

# Setting up the evidence pipeline

Do the steps in order. Step 2 has to happen before any AI tool touches the repo.

## 0. Installs (each teammate, once)

- Git and Python 3.8 or newer
- Foundry: `curl -L https://foundry.paradigm.xyz | bash`, then `foundryup`
- Slither: `python3 -m pip install slither-analyzer`
- Your git name, which is recorded on every evidence run and AI session: `git config --global user.name "Your Name"`

If `python3` is not the command for Python on your machine, change the two `"python3"` entries in `.claude/settings.json`.

## 1. Create the repo

Make it a **private** GitHub repo. AI transcripts are committed, and they can contain anything that was typed into a session. Clone it.

## 2. Commit spec v0 first, on its own

Unzip this kit into the repo root. Fill in "Date written" and "Written by" in `docs/spec/spec-v0.md`. Then:

```bash
git add docs/spec/spec-v0.md
git commit -m "docs: spec v0 (pre-AI proposal)"
git tag spec-v0
git add -A
git commit -m "chore: evidence pipeline"
git push --follow-tags
```

Be honest about what this proves. Git commit dates can be set to anything, so the tag alone is weak evidence. The strong evidence is the date you submitted the BYOP proposal to the coordinator, so put that date in the file.

## 3. Log today's research chat

Copy the claude.ai conversation from 23 Oct 2026 into `docs/ai-logs/exports/2026-10-23-claude-ai-research.md`. Its row in `docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md` is already filled in.

## 4. Start Claude Code and check the hook

From the repo root run `claude -n toolchain-setup`. Accept the trust prompt for the folder if one appears. Run `/hooks`: it should list a `Stop` hook and a `SessionEnd` hook from project settings. After Claude's first reply, `docs/ai-logs/raw/` should contain a `.jsonl` file. If it doesn't, stop and fix that first, because every session before the fix is lost evidence.

## 5. Paste this prompt into Claude Code

```text
Read CLAUDE.md first. Set up the Foundry toolchain for this repo. Do not write any contract code: spec-v1 is not frozen.

1. Check that forge and slither are installed (forge --version, slither --version). If either is missing, stop and tell me. Don't install them yourself.
2. Run `forge init --force` in the repo root. Then run `git status` and make sure it did not change .gitignore, CLAUDE.md, SETUP.md, slither.config.json, or anything under docs/, scripts/ or .claude/. Restore anything it changed.
3. Install OpenZeppelin Contracts pinned to the latest v5.x release tag. Find the tag with `git ls-remote --tags https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts`, then `forge install OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts@<tag>`. Write remappings with `forge remappings > remappings.txt`.
4. Make the scripts executable: chmod +x scripts/*.sh .claude/hooks/archive_transcript.py
5. Run `scripts/evidence.sh pipeline-check` and show me summary.txt. build, test, gas and coverage should exit 0. Slither exits non-zero only if it reports findings.
6. Delete src/Counter.sol, test/Counter.t.sol and script/Counter.s.sol so the AI baseline starts from an empty src/.
7. Commit everything as "chore: foundry toolchain and OpenZeppelin <tag>". Do not push.

Then tell me what you did and anything that did not go as described.
```

## 6. After the session

Run `/export docs/ai-logs/exports/<date>-toolchain-setup.txt` before you quit. Add a row to `docs/ai-logs/INDEX.md`. Commit and push.

## Later: creating the AI baseline

Once `spec-v1.md` has no `TODO(decision)` left, generate the first full version of the contracts on its own branch and freeze it:

```bash
git switch -c ai-baseline
# ...AI generates the code; commit it as-is with an "ai:" prefix...
git tag ai-baseline
git switch main
git merge ai-baseline
```

All review and fixes happen on `main`. `ai-baseline` is never edited again; it is your Report Section 4 and the "before" for every issue.

## Notes

- `forge init` also adds a GitHub Actions workflow in `.github/workflows/`. Keep it. CI runs on GitHub's servers give you timestamped test results that nobody on the team can edit. Its `forge fmt --check` step will fail on unformatted code; run `forge fmt` before pushing.
- Slither does not catch everything. In testing this kit, a function that let anyone whitelist themselves passed Slither with no warning; only a unit test caught it. Tests are the main line of defence and Slither is a supplement.

# Spec v0: original proposal (pre-AI)

This is the team's proposal as written before any AI tool was used. It is the baseline for Report Section 1 (Initial Specification & System Scope).

Do not edit this file. It is tagged `spec-v0`. All changes go in `spec-v1.md`.

Date written: <!-- fill in: when the team wrote this proposal -->
Written by: <!-- fill in: team member names -->

---

Tokenisation of Real-World and Digital Assets on Ethereum

The project would be inspired by the increasing adoption of asset tokenisation by major financial institutions such as BlackRock, J.P. Morgan, and DTCC. We aim to develop a simplified dApp demonstrating how traditionally managed assets can be represented, issued, transferred, and managed using blockchain-based tokens and smart contracts.

For our proposed MVP, we are considering the following features:

Asset tokenisation: An authorised issuer can create/tokenise an asset using an Ethereum token standard.
Investor wallet interaction: Users can connect their wallets and view their tokenised asset holdings.
Primary issuance and transfer: Users can acquire and transfer tokenised assets through smart contracts.
Ownership and transaction records: Asset ownership and transaction history are maintained transparently on-chain.
Issuer controls/compliance: Basic mechanisms such as whitelisting authorised investors or restricting transfers to approved addresses.
From a technical perspective, we plan to implement the system using Solidity smart contracts on Ethereum, together with a web-based frontend and wallet integration such as MetaMask. We would also explore relevant token standards and smart-contract mechanisms used for tokenised financial assets.

The broader problem we would like to explore is how blockchain can provide programmable ownership, transparent settlement, and more efficient transfer of assets, while also accounting for the permissioning and compliance requirements that distinguish institutional asset tokenisation from ordinary cryptocurrencies.

# run is supposed to show a failing test.

set -uo pipefail

root=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || { echo "Run this inside the git repo." >&2; exit 1; }
cd "$root"

label="${1:-}"
sha=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo nocommit)
dirty=""
if [ -n "$(git status --porcelain --untracked-files=no 2>/dev/null)" ]; then
  dirty="-dirty"
fi
ts=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
out="docs/evidence/runs/${ts}_${sha}${dirty}${label:+_$label}"
mkdir -p "$out"

{
  echo "utc: $ts"
  echo "commit: $(git rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo none)"
  echo "uncommitted changes: ${dirty:+yes}${dirty:-no}"
  echo "label: ${label:-none}"
  echo "run by: $(git config user.name 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)"
  echo "forge: $(forge --version 2>/dev/null | head -n 1)"
  echo "slither: $(slither --version 2>/dev/null)"
} > "$out/meta.txt"

: > "$out/summary.txt"

step() {
  local name=$1; shift
  echo ">> $name: $*"

}

# with a quote and are dropped from the checklist.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Copy the current Claude Code transcript into docs/ai-logs/raw/.

Claude Code runs this on Stop (after every turn, in the background) and on
SessionEnd. It reads the hook's JSON input from stdin, copies the session's
transcript file into the repo, and records the session in sessions.tsv the
first time it sees it. Claude Code deletes its own copy of old transcripts,
so this copy is the one we keep.

It always exits 0 so it can never block Claude Code.
"""
import datetime
import json
import os
import pathlib
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys


def git_user(root):
    try:
        out = subprocess.run(
            ["git", "config", "user.name"],
            cwd=root, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=5,
        )
        return out.stdout.strip() or "unknown"
    except Exception:
        return "unknown"


def main():
    try:
        data = json.load(sys.stdin)
    except Exception:
        return
    src = data.get("transcript_path")
    session_id = data.get("session_id") or "unknown"
    if not src or not os.path.isfile(src):
        return

    root = os.environ.get("CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR") or data.get("cwd") or os.getcwd()
    raw_dir = pathlib.Path(root, "docs", "ai-logs", "raw")
    raw_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    existing = sorted(raw_dir.glob(f"*_{session_id}.jsonl"))
    if existing:
        dest = existing[0]
    else:
        stamp = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).strftime("%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ")
        dest = raw_dir / f"{stamp}_{session_id}.jsonl"

    shutil.copyfile(src, dest)

    if not existing:
        tsv = raw_dir.parent / "sessions.tsv"
        new_file = not tsv.exists()
        with open(tsv, "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            if new_file:
                f.write("first_seen_utc\tsession_id\tgit_user\ttranscript\n")
            f.write(f"{dest.name.split('_')[0]}\t{session_id}\t{git_user(root)}\traw/{dest.name}\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        main()
    except Exception:
        pass
    sys.exit(0)

# Phase 1 — Project Foundation and Architecture

## Context

SC4053 NTU project: tokenised-asset dApp + AI Audit Report. The evidence kit (now extracted to `sc4053-evidence-kit/`) provides the grading scaffold (issue tracking, evidence runs, AI session logging). The user confirmed Hardhat as the smart-contract toolchain (not Foundry), so the `evidence.sh` forge-based pipeline is retained in `docs/` but won't produce live CI output; grading evidence will come from Hardhat test logs and manual exports.

Phase 1 goal: freeze `spec-v1.md`, copy the evidence kit into the repo root, initialise Hardhat, and commit the empty-contracts skeleton so every later phase starts from a reviewable baseline.

---

## Step 1 — Copy evidence kit to repo root

Copy all files from `sc4053-evidence-kit/` into the repo root (same tree, no subfolder rename). Files to copy:
- `.claude/` (hooks + settings.json)
- `docs/` (spec, ai-logs, issues, evidence, report)
- `scripts/evidence.sh`, `scripts/new-issue.sh`
- `.env.example`
- `.gitignore` (merge with any existing)
- `CLAUDE.md`
- `SETUP.md`
- `slither.config.json`

**Critical**: do NOT delete `sc4053-evidence-kit/` yet — copy first, verify, then it can be left or deleted.

---

## Step 2 — Fill in spec-v0.md

Edit `docs/spec/spec-v0.md`:
```
Date written: 23 October 2026
Written by: Chordia Laksh
```

---

## Step 3 — First commit + tag

```
git add docs/spec/spec-v0.md
git commit -m "docs: spec v0 (pre-AI proposal)"
git tag spec-v0
```

Then:
```
git add -A
git commit -m "chore: evidence pipeline"
```

---

## Step 4 — Fill in spec-v1.md (freeze it)

Replace every `TODO(decision)` with the Phase 1 decisions below. Every section must be written so the spec has no `TODO(decision)` markers remaining.

### Section 1 — Problem and trust model
- Problem: real-world asset ownership is opaque, settlement slow, and compliance manual.
- Why blockchain: immutable on-chain ownership record, programmable transfer rules (whitelist), atomic settlement via smart contract removes counterparty risk.
- Trust model: the issuer is trusted to correctly describe the off-chain asset; the on-chain token is a share register only — the legal claim sits off-chain.
- Out of trust scope: oracle price accuracy, issuer solvency.

### Section 2 — Asset and scope
Instrument: **fictional real estate investment fund** — Campus Property Fund.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Token name | Campus Property Token |
| Symbol | CPT |
| Total supply | 10 000 CPT |
| Token decimals | 0 (whole units) |
| Initial sale price | 0.001 testnet ETH / token |
| Issuer | MetaMask Wallet A |
| Investor 1 | MetaMask Wallet B |
| Investor 2 | MetaMask Wallet C |

A second demo asset (Digital Licensing Revenue Pool / DLP) reuses the same contracts with different metadata.

### Section 3 — Roles
| Actor | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Platform admin | authorise/deauthorise issuer wallets | hold tokens, buy assets |
| Authorised issuer | create assets, set sale price at creation, whitelist investors, allocate tokens to sale, withdraw ETH proceeds, freeze individual investor | control another issuer's assets |
| Investor | connect wallet, buy tokens from whitelisted sale, transfer tokens to other whitelisted investors, view own balance | buy if not whitelisted |

### Section 4 — Contracts and state

**AssetToken.sol**
- ERC-20 implementation (OpenZeppelin ERC20 base)
- State: `mapping(address => bool) public whitelist`, `address public issuer`, `bool public paused`, `mapping(address => bool) public frozen`
- Calls: none external
- Price model: **fixed price set at deployment** (stored in AssetSale, not AssetToken)
- Extra features in scope: whitelist (required to receive/send), pause (issuer can halt all transfers), freeze (issuer can freeze one address), forced transfer (issuer can move tokens from frozen address)
- Out of scope: redemption, yield, NAV oracle

**AssetFactory.sol**
- State: `mapping(address => bool) public authorisedIssuers`, `address[] public assets`, `mapping(address => address) public tokenToSale`
- Calls: deploys AssetToken and AssetSale
- Admin: platform admin address set in constructor

**AssetSale.sol**
- State: `AssetToken public token`, `uint256 public priceWei`, `address public issuer`
- DvP design: **escrow** — issuer calls `allocate(amount)` to transfer tokens in; investor calls `buy(amount)` payable; ETH held in contract; issuer calls `withdrawProceeds()`.
- Subscription flow: **instant** — `buy` reverts if investor not whitelisted, otherwise transfers tokens and holds ETH immediately.

### Section 5 — Functions (key ones)

| Function | Who | Preconditions | Effects | Reverts if |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `AssetFactory.authoriseIssuer(addr)` | admin | addr not yet authorised | adds to authorisedIssuers | caller != admin |
| `AssetFactory.createAsset(name, symbol, supply, priceWei)` | authorised issuer | issuer is authorised | deploys AssetToken + AssetSale, mints supply to issuer, records in registry | caller not authorised |
| `AssetToken.addToWhitelist(addr)` | issuer | — | whitelist[addr] = true | caller != issuer |
| `AssetToken.transfer(to, amount)` | token holder | to is whitelisted, not paused, neither party frozen | standard ERC-20 transfer | any precondition false |
| `AssetSale.allocate(amount)` | issuer | issuer holds >= amount tokens | transfers tokens into AssetSale | caller != issuer |
| `AssetSale.buy(amount)` | investor | investor is whitelisted, msg.value == amount * priceWei, enough tokens in sale | transfers tokens to investor, holds ETH | any precondition false |
| `AssetSale.withdrawProceeds()` | issuer | — | sends ETH balance to issuer | caller != issuer |
| `AssetToken.pause()` / `unpause()` | issuer | — | paused flag | caller != issuer |
| `AssetToken.freeze(addr)` / `unfreeze(addr)` | issuer | — | frozen flag | caller != issuer |

### Section 6 — Invariants
1. Every address with a non-zero CPT balance is on the AssetToken whitelist.
2. `AssetToken.totalSupply()` equals the sum of all balances.
3. ETH held by AssetSale equals (tokens sold from AssetSale) × priceWei, minus any withdrawn proceeds.
4. No non-whitelisted address ever receives a token transfer (reverts at ERC-20 hook level).
5. Only the issuer who deployed an AssetToken can modify its whitelist, paused state, or frozen addresses.

### Section 7 — Frontend
Three pages:
- **Admin dashboard**: list of authorised issuers, button to authorise/remove.
- **Issuer dashboard**: create new asset (form), list own assets, per-asset: allocate tokens to sale, whitelist investor address, view proceeds, withdraw.
- **Investor dashboard**: list of available assets (from factory registry), buy tokens (enter amount, pay ETH), view own balances, transfer to another address.

Each screen connects via MetaMask (ethers.js `BrowserProvider`).

### Section 8 — Out of scope
- NFT-based unique assets — out of scope for MVP simplicity
- Redemption / buyback — out of scope
- Yield / dividend distribution — out of scope
- NAV oracle / price updates after creation — out of scope
- Multi-jurisdiction compliance rules beyond a single whitelist — out of scope
- Actual legal enforceability of the on-chain record — out of scope

### Section 9 — Assumptions
- Network: Sepolia testnet (chain ID 11155111)
- Decimals: 0 (whole tokens only, matches fractional-unit model)
- Test wallets: three Hardhat accounts in local network; three MetaMask burner wallets on Sepolia
- Node.js >= 18, Hardhat 2.x, OpenZeppelin Contracts 5.x
- Frontend: React 18, ethers.js 6.x, Vite

### Section 10 — Changes from v0
| Change | Why | AI influence |
|---|---|---|
| Narrowed to one real estate fund + one digital asset | MVP focus | No |
| Three concrete contracts (Token, Factory, Sale) | Clarifies separation of concerns | AI research session 2026-10-23 (exports/2026-10-23-claude-ai-research.md) |
| Fixed price model (not NAV) | Simplicity for MVP | No |
| Instant subscription (not request-and-approve) | Reduces contract complexity | No |
| Whitelist + pause + freeze as in-scope features | Matches institutional compliance requirement from v0 | No |

---

## Step 5 — npm init + Hardhat + OpenZeppelin

Run in repo root:
```
npm init -y
npm install --save-dev hardhat @nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox
npm install @openzeppelin/contracts
npx hardhat init   # choose "Create a JavaScript project", accept defaults
```

`hardhat.config.js` networks: local hardhat network + Sepolia (RPC URL from .env).

Update `.gitignore` to include `node_modules/`, `cache/`, `artifacts/`, `coverage/`, `.env`.

---

## Step 6 — Create contract skeleton files

Create stub files (empty but compilable) in `contracts/`:

**`contracts/AssetToken.sol`** — ERC-20 stub (imports OpenZeppelin ERC20, constructor, empty body)
**`contracts/AssetFactory.sol`** — stub (constructor with admin address)
**`contracts/AssetSale.sol`** — stub (constructor with token address and priceWei)

These stubs must compile with `npx hardhat compile`. Full implementations come in Phase 2.

---

## Step 7 — Create test, scripts, frontend stubs

- `test/AssetToken.test.js` — empty describe block, `it.skip` placeholders
- `test/AssetFactory.test.js` — same
- `test/AssetSale.test.js` — same
- `scripts/deploy.js` — commented-out deploy scaffold
- `scripts/setupDemo.js` — commented-out demo scaffold
- `frontend/` — `npm create vite@latest frontend -- --template react` (or just mkdir + package.json stub)

---

## Step 8 — Commit

```
git add docs/spec/spec-v1.md
git commit -m "docs: spec v1 frozen — Campus Property Fund, fixed price, instant subscription"

git add -A
git commit -m "chore: hardhat toolchain, OpenZeppelin 5.x, contract stubs"
```

Then push.

---

## Verification

Phase 1 completion criteria:
- [ ] `git tag spec-v0` exists and points to spec-v0.md commit
- [ ] `docs/spec/spec-v1.md` has zero `TODO(decision)` markers
- [ ] `npx hardhat compile` exits 0 (contracts compile)
- [ ] `npx hardhat test` runs (all tests skip/pass, none error)
- [ ] `ls frontend/` is non-empty
- [ ] All team members can `git clone && npm install && npx hardhat compile`

---

## Notes

- The `scripts/evidence.sh` file calls `forge` which is not installed. It is kept for the grading scaffold but will only work if Foundry is installed later. The report should note Hardhat as the primary testing toolchain.
- `CLAUDE.md` rule: do not write contract code until spec-v1 has no `TODO(decision)` — satisfied by Step 4 before Step 6.

- Actions visible to others or that affect shared state: pushing code, creating/closing/commenting on PRs or issues, sending messages (Slack, email, GitHub), posting to external services, modifying shared infrastructure or permissions
- Uploading content to third-party web tools (diagram renderers, pastebins, gists) publishes it - consider whether it could be sensitive before sending, since it may be cached or indexed even if later deleted.

When you encounter an obstacle, do not use destructive actions as a shortcut to simply make it go away. For instance, try to identify root causes and fix underlying issues rather than bypassing safety checks (e.g. --no-verify). If you discover unexpected state like unfamiliar files, branches, or configuration, investigate before deleting or overwriting, as it may represent the user's in-progress work. If you're unsure whether the user would want something kept, prefer a reversible step (move it aside, rename it, or stash it) over deleting; files you created yourself this session (scratch outputs, experiment intermediates) are yours to clean up freely. For example, typically resolve merge conflicts rather than discarding changes; similarly, if a lock file exists, investigate what process holds it rather than deleting it. In a git repository, run `git status` before any command that could discard uncommitted work (git checkout/restore/reset/clean, rm -rf on a repo path, restoring from a snapshot), and stash (with `-u` for untracked) or commit anything you find first. And when staging or committing: review what's included (`git status` after a broad `git add`), and if you see anything suspicious that might reveal secrets — even if the filename looks innocuous — double-check the file's contents before pushing. In short: only take risky actions carefully, and when in doubt, ask before acting. Follow both the spirit and letter of these instructions - measure twice, cut once.

 - Use TaskCreate to plan and track work. Mark each task completed as soon as it's done; don't batch.
 - You can call multiple tools in a single response. If you intend to call multiple tools and there are no dependencies between them, make all independent tool calls in parallel. Maximize use of parallel tool calls where possible to increase efficiency. However, if some tool calls depend on previous calls to inform dependent values, do NOT call these tools in parallel and instead call them sequentially. For instance, if one operation must complete before another starts, run these operations sequentially instead.

 - When referencing specific functions or pieces of code include the pattern file_path:line_number to allow the user to easily navigate to the source code location.

To make a small change to a page you already published with the Artifact tool in this conversation, send it as `edits` (old_str/new_str pairs copied exactly from the file as it now stands) on an Artifact publish of the same `file_path`: that one call changes the file and the page together, with no Read and no Edit. For a change to several files at once, or a rewrite of most of a page, use Edit on the file(s), not a shell command, and publish the artifact again with the same `file_path` in the same response: the Edit call(s) first, then the Artifact publish, with no Read and without waiting for the Edit result. The calls run in the order sent, so the publish carries the edited file; a publish sent in the same response as a failed Edit of that file is refused and leaves the artifact as it was, so correct the Edit and publish again. Either way, read the file first only if its text is not in this conversation or you can't place the change exactly from it.

Assume users can't see most tool calls or thinking — only your text output. Before your first tool call, state in one sentence what you're about to do. While working, give short updates at key moments: when you find something, when you change direction, or when you hit a blocker. Brief is good — silent is not. One sentence per update is almost always enough.

Don't narrate your internal deliberation. User-facing text should be relevant communication to the user, not a running commentary on your thought process. State results and decisions directly, and focus user-facing text on relevant updates for the user.

When you do write updates, write so the reader can pick up cold: complete sentences, no unexplained jargon or shorthand from earlier in the session. But keep it tight — a clear sentence is better than a clear paragraph.

End-of-turn summary: one or two sentences. What changed and what's next. Nothing else.

Match responses to the task: a simple question gets a direct answer, not headers and sections.

In code: default to writing no comments. Never write multi-paragraph docstrings or multi-line comment blocks — one short line max. Don't create planning, decision, or analysis documents unless the user asks for them — work from conversation context, not intermediate files.

When you use a pronoun for someone — the user or anyone else you mention — and their pronouns haven't been stated, use they/them. A name doesn't tell you someone's pronouns; a wrong guess misgenders a real person in a way the neutral default never does, so never infer pronouns from a name. ## What NOT to save in memory

- Code patterns, conventions, architecture, file paths, or project structure — these can be derived by reading the current project state.
- Git history, recent changes, or who-changed-what — `git log` / `git blame` are authoritative.
- Debugging solutions or fix recipes — the fix is in the code; the commit message has the context.
- Anything already documented in CLAUDE.md files.
- Ephemeral task details: in-progress work, temporary state, current conversation context.

These exclusions apply even when the user explicitly asks you to save. If they ask you to save a PR list or activity summary, ask what was *surprising* or *non-obvious* about it — that is the part worth keeping.

## How to save memories

Saving a memory is a two-step process:

**Step 1** — write the memory to its own file (e.g., `user_role.md`, `feedback_testing.md`) using this frontmatter format:

```markdown
---
name: {{short-kebab-case-slug}}
description: {{one-line summary, used to decide relevance in future conversations, so be specific}}
metadata:
  type: {{user, feedback, project, reference}}
---

{{memory content — for feedback/project types, structure as: rule/fact, then **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines. Link related memories with [[their-name]].}}
```

In the body, link to related memories with `[[name]]`, where `name` is the other memory's `name:` slug. Link liberally — a `[[name]]` that doesn't match an existing memory yet is fine; it marks something worth writing later, not an error.

**Step 2** — add a pointer to that file in `MEMORY.md`. `MEMORY.md` is an index, not a memory — each entry should be one line, under ~150 characters: `- [Title](file.md) — one-line hook`. It has no frontmatter. Never write memory content directly into `MEMORY.md`.

- `MEMORY.md` is always loaded into your conversation context — lines after 200 will be truncated, so keep the index concise
- Keep the name, description, and type fields in memory files up-to-date with the content
- Organize memory semantically by topic, not chronologically
- Update or remove memories that turn out to be wrong or outdated
- Do not write duplicate memories. First check if there is an existing memory you can update before writing a new one.

## When to access memories
- When memories seem relevant, or the user references prior-conversation work.
- You MUST access memory when the user explicitly asks you to check, recall, or remember.
- If the user says to *ignore* or *not use* memory: Do not apply remembered facts, cite, compare against, or mention memory content.
- Memory records can become stale over time. Use memory as context for what was true at a given point in time. Before answering the user or building assumptions based solely on information in memory records, verify that the memory is still correct and up-to-date by reading the current state of the files or resources. If a recalled memory conflicts with current information, trust what you observe now — and update or remove the stale memory rather than acting on it.

## Before recommending from memory

A memory that names a specific function, file, or flag is a claim that it existed *when the memory was written*. It may have been renamed, removed, or never merged. Before recommending it:

- If the memory names a file path: check the file exists.
- If the memory names a function or flag: grep for it.
- If the user is about to act on your recommendation (not just asking about history), verify first.

"The memory says X exists" is not the same as "X exists now."

A memory that summarizes repo state (activity logs, architecture snapshots) is frozen in time. If the user asks about *recent* or *current* state, prefer `git log` or reading the code over recalling the snapshot.

## Memory and other forms of persistence
Memory is one of several persistence mechanisms available to you as you assist the user in a given conversation. The distinction is often that memory can be recalled in future conversations and should not be used for persisting information that is only useful within the scope of the current conversation.
- When to use or update a plan instead of memory: If you are about to start a non-trivial implementation task and would like to reach alignment with the user on your approach you should use a Plan rather than saving this information to memory. Similarly, if you already have a plan within the conversation and you have changed your approach persist that change by updating the plan rather than saving a memory.
- When to use or update tasks instead of memory: When you need to break your work in current conversation into discrete steps or keep track of your progress use tasks instead of saving to memory. Tasks are great for persisting information about the work that needs to be done in the current conversation, but memory should be reserved for information that will be useful in future conversations.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

**Do not spawn agents unless the user asks.** Each spawn starts cold and re-derives context you already have — it's the expensive path on this plan. A task with "multiple angles," "thorough," or several parts is not a request to spawn; handle it inline with your own tools. Only use this tool when the user explicitly says to use a subagent, or names one of the available agent types.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## Usage notes

- Always include a short description summarizing what the agent will do
- When the agent is done, its final report is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Trust but verify: an agent's summary describes what it intended to do, not necessarily what it did. When an agent writes or edits code, check the actual changes before reporting the work as done.
- To continue a previously spawned agent, use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name as the `to` field — that resumes it with full context. A new Agent call starts a fresh agent with no memory of prior runs (except subagent_type: "fork"), so the prompt must be self-contained.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tool access are set in its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter, or the SDK `agents` option); the `model` parameter here overrides the definition for this one call.
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since a fresh agent is not aware of the user's intent
- If the agent description mentions that it should be used proactively, then you should try your best to use it without the user having to ask for it first.
- If the user specifies that they want you to run agents "in parallel", you MUST send a single message with multiple Agent tool use content blocks. For example, if you need to launch both a build-validator agent and a test-runner agent in parallel, send a single message with both tool calls.
- With `isolation: "worktree"`, the worktree is automatically cleaned up if the agent makes no changes; otherwise the path and branch are returned in the result.

## When to fork

Fork yourself (pass `subagent_type: "fork"`) when the intermediate tool output isn't worth keeping in your context. The criterion is qualitative — "will I need this output again" — not task size. Fork open-ended questions. If research can be broken into independent questions, launch parallel forks in one message. A fork beats a fresh subagent for this — it inherits context and shares your cache.

Forks are cheap because they share your prompt cache.

**Don't peek.** The tool result includes an `output_file` path — do not Read or tail it. You get a completion notification; trust it. Reading the transcript mid-flight pulls the fork's tool noise into your context, which defeats the point of forking.

**Don't race.** After launching, you know nothing about what the fork found. Never fabricate or predict fork results in any format — not as prose, summary, or structured output. The notification arrives as a user-role message in a later turn; it is never something you write yourself. If the user asks a follow-up before the notification lands, tell them the fork is still running — give status, not a guess.

**Writing a fork prompt.** Since the fork inherits your context, the prompt is a *directive* — what to do, not what the situation is. Be specific about scope: what's in, what's out, what another agent is handling. Don't re-explain background.


## Writing the prompt

Any agent other than a fork starts with zero context. Brief the agent like a smart colleague who just walked into the room — it hasn't seen this conversation, doesn't know what you've tried, doesn't understand why this task matters.
- Explain what you're trying to accomplish and why.
- Describe what you've already learned or ruled out.
- Give enough context about the surrounding problem that the agent can make judgment calls rather than just following a narrow instruction.
- If you need a short response, say so ("report in under 200 words").
- Lookups: hand over the exact command. Investigations: hand over the question — prescribed steps become dead weight when the premise is wrong.

For fresh agents, terse command-style prompts produce shallow, generic work.

**Never delegate understanding.** Don't write "based on your findings, fix the bug" or "based on the research, implement it." Those phrases push synthesis onto the agent instead of doing it yourself. Write prompts that prove you understood: include file paths, line numbers, what specifically to change.

Example usage:

user: "What's left on this branch before we can ship?"
assistant: <thinking>Forking this — it's a survey question. I want the punch list, not the git output in my context.</thinking>
Agent({
  subagent_type: "fork",
  name: "ship-audit",
  description: "Branch ship-readiness audit",
  prompt: "Audit what's left before this branch can ship. Check: uncommitted changes, commits ahead of main, whether tests exist, whether the GrowthBook gate is wired up, whether CI-relevant files changed. Report a punch list — done vs. missing. Under 200 words."
})
assistant: Ship-readiness audit running.
<commentary>
Turn ends here. The coordinator knows nothing about the findings yet. What follows is a SEPARATE turn — the notification arrives from outside, as a user-role message. It is not something the coordinator writes.
</commentary>
[later turn — notification arrives as user message]
assistant: Audit's back. Three blockers: no tests for the new prompt path, GrowthBook gate wired but not in build_flags.yaml, and one uncommitted file.
</example>

<example>
user: "so is the gate wired up or not"
<commentary>
User asks mid-wait. The audit fork was launched to answer exactly this, and it hasn't returned. The coordinator does not have this answer. Give status, not a fabricated result.
</commentary>
assistant: Still waiting on the audit — that's one of the things it's checking. Should land shortly.
</example>

<example>
user: "Can you get a second opinion on whether this migration is safe?"
assistant: <thinking>I'll ask the code-reviewer agent — it won't see my analysis, so it can give an independent read.</thinking>
<commentary>
A non-fork subagent_type is specified, so the agent starts fresh. It needs full context in the prompt. The briefing explains what to assess and why.
</commentary>

  name: "migration-review",
  description: "Independent migration review",
  subagent_type: "code-reviewer",
  prompt: "Review migration 0042_user_schema.sql for safety. Context: we're adding a NOT NULL column to a 50M-row table. Existing rows get a backfill default. I want a second opinion on whether the backfill approach is safe under concurrent writes — I've checked locking behavior but want independent verification.
